articles.title: No bail for P-plater over Newcastle crash that left five-year-old in induced coma and injured nine other NRL fans
articles.summary:
Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to farewell their team

  • Get our
articles.byline: Australian Associated Press and Andrew Messenger

blocks.text: A driver whose car careered into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters – leaving children as young as five injured – will be kept in custody as the community rallies to support those hospitalised after the crash.
Ten people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout on Saturday morning.

Six people remain at the John Hunter hospital with injuries caused by the collision, according to the Hunter New England Local Health District chief executive, Tracey McCosker. Two are in a serious condition, while four are stable.
They include a five-year-old girl who had been placed into an induced coma with critical injuries, although her condition has stabilised.

Samarasinghe was taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences, including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.
He did not make any application for release during a brief court appearance on Sunday, and he was formally refused bail. The judge also endorsed a warrant for a health assessment.
The bail court was told the most serious offence of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm carried a maximum jail term of seven years.
He will next appear at the Newcastle local court on 15 October.

Chris Clancy was among those injured in the crash, after joining thousands of Newcastle Knights fans to lined the streets to farewell their team as the players travelled to Sydney for the grand final.
“We’re there at the roundabout having fun – cars going past, beeping their horns, people waving,” Clancy said.
“The next thing, this car stops [at] the roundabout and then he just floored it on the wet ground, lost it.
“It happened in seconds, but when you stand there, seeing the car coming at you, I honestly thought I was going to die. It just felt like slow motion.”
Clancy suffered small fractures in his ribs and spine, a broken collarbone, and small fractures in his foot.
after newsletter promotion
Investigators did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was being driven erratically before the crash.
Multiple fundraisers have been established for the victims of the incident, including one for the five-year-old girl and another for Wallsend grandfather Dave Martin.
Martin was injured after being struck by the car while trying to protect his two young granddaughters, sustaining multiple fractures in both legs and undergoing a lengthy surgery.
He was known in Wallsend for his love of the Knights, often decorating his barber shop on Nelson Street with team paraphernalia.
The Knights’ chief executive, Peter Parr, expressed deep concern for those affected by the crash.
“Newcastle is a strong community,” he said.
“We have seen that strength throughout this week, and today we need to draw on it again with compassion, care and support for those who need it most.”

articles.title: Juno-winning singer Sass Jordan dead at 65
articles.summary: A post on Jordan's social media page on Saturday says she died the day before "surrounded by her loving family." It called her an "inimitable force of nature" and "irreplaceable being of light and…

image.caption: Jordan was born in Birmingham, England, and raised in Montreal. (CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment

A post on Jordan's social media page on Saturday says she died the day before "surrounded by her loving family." It called her an "inimitable force of nature" and "irreplaceable being of light and joy."
Cause of death has not been released
Sass Jordan, the Montreal-raised rock singer whose career spanned nearly four decades, has died at 65.
Jordan died Friday surrounded by those who loved her most, said a statement from family spokesperson Eric Alper.
The statement described Jordan as an inimitable force of nature and an irreplaceable being of light and joy.
A cause of death has not been released.

Jordan's debut album, Tell Somebody, was released in 1988, and she won the Juno Award for most promising female vocalist of the year in 1989. Her second album, Racine, released in 1992, included hits like Make You a Believer.
She was nominated several times for a Juno Award for best female vocalist. She was also a judge on all six seasons of the reality television competition show Canadian Idol.

items: Then and now: Sass Jordan on the 30th anniversary of Tell Somebody

blocks.text: 'Really belt out the blues'
She was born on Dec. 23, 1960 in Birmingham, England, and raised in Montreal, according to the statement.
Geoff Kulawick, former president of Stony Plain Records, which released Jordan's last two albums, described her as "bold, beautiful and brave."
Jordan recorded her 2020 album, Rebel Moon Blues, and her 2022 album, Bitches Blues, with her husband Derek Sharp while signed with Stony Plains.
Kulawick said he was a fan even before Jordan signed to his label, and that he convinced her she could "really belt out the blues" on her final two records.
"Her voice really stood out and the way she was able to connect emotionally … brought her tons of fans," he said.
An inspiration to all young performers
Canadian producer and songwriter Derek Downham said they "really hit it off" when they first met at Toronto's Massey Hall a few years ago.
"She was a ray of light and a really hilarious person," said Downham, who also played drums alongside Jordan last December at singer-songwriter Andy Kim's annual holiday charity concert in Montreal.
"The biggest heartbreak for me is that I won't get to see that laugh again."
As one of the few women in rock when she started out, Jordan helped make space for other woman in a male-dominated genre, he said.
"She was coming up in a time where it wasn't easy," he said. "It's nice to see a strong female poke through and really show people how it's done."

items: Sass Jordan says she thinks of 'music as medicine' and she still loves to connect with fans

blocks.text: Downham said Jordan was an inspiration to all young performers.
"I hope that people remember her for leading the way and that she led with love every time."

articles.title: Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1
articles.summary: One person has died and two others have suffered burns in a fire near the main access route to the historic sanctuary of Machu Picchu.

image.caption: The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century Image: Laurent Davoust/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: A blaze was burning near the main access road to the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu in Peru, leaving one person dead and two injured, officials said on Saturday.
The fire began on Friday in the Sacred Valley of the Cusco region, which also includes the Ollantaytambo train station — the busiest for travelers visiting Machu Picchu.
"We have one elderly person who died in the flames and two others with second-degree burns," Miguel Osco, head of the Cusco Regional Office for Disaster Management and Safety, told RPP radio.
How did the fire start?
Osco said the fire originated from controlled bush burning that farmers carry out to clear land for crops.
The flames spread quickly because of the hot, windy weather and dry vegetation, he added.
The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century.
Located at an altitude of 2,500 meters in the Andes Mountains, the historic sanctuary is regarded as an architectural masterpiece.
UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983.
Machu Picchu is Peru's most famous tourist destination, attracting about three million visitors every year.

articles.title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
articles.summary: Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.

blocks.text: Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.

Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.

The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.

"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.

Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.

''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.

The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

articles.title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
articles.summary: Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations of a woman who says she was drugged and gang raped as "deeply disturbing".

blocks.text: Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house.
In an eight-minute video statement released Saturday evening, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing".
The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said.

Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024.
She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid.
Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.
Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better".
"We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said.
He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity".
As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life".
"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case.
Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to leaddddd a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter.
Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

articles.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.

Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.

A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.

But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.

In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."

Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

articles.title: US father and son arrested after 'gas station heroin' deaths
articles.summary: They are accused of selling at least one student derivatives of kratom, often called "gas station heroin" in the US.

blocks.text: A father and son who worked at a Mississippi smoke shop have been arrested and charged in connection with the death of at least one university student who died from a suspected overdose of kratom, sometimes called "gas station heroin" in the US.
The pair worked at a shop that allegedly sold derivatives of the substance to University of Mississippi students.

US prosecutors charged Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, for possession with the intent to distribute controlled substances in connection with the death investigation of two Ole Miss students last month.
Although their deaths have not officially been attributed to kratom, officials afterward issued warnings about consuming kratom.

The criminal complaint alleges that on 21 September, an Ole Miss student was found dead in his dorm room. The apparent cause of death "appeared to be consistent with a drug overdose", the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi said in a press release.
Law enforcement found packages - with some tablets missing - of suspected kratom derivatives.
About an hour later, a second student was found dead from a suspected overdose in another location, also with packages of suspected kratom derivatives.
Officials connected the packages with the local vape, tobacco and beer store, the US Attorney's statement said.
Law enforcement executed search warrants and seized suspected kratom derivative controlled substances from the store. The Mosleh's, father and son, were later arrested.
The two students' deaths have sparked alarm and warnings from officials about the plant-based drug referred to as "gas station heroin".
Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.

For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it is illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.

The Mississippi prosecutors said that kratom derivatives, such as MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16, are now schedule I controlled substances in the US and can be significantly more potent than natural kratom leaf products and morphine.

articles.title: AI giants 'not being nearly careful enough,' warns outgoing OpenAI safety engineer
articles.summary: Days after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence giants, a former OpenAI worker said his industry needs the same safeguards as nuclear power or aviation.

image.caption: OpenAI has delayed plans for a public listing this year due to safety concernsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A safety engineer who recently quit ChatGPTcreator OpenAI warned Saturday that artificial intelligence (AI) firms were "not being nearly careful enough."
David Robinson's comments come amid growing concerns about AI becoming too powerful — a threat that US President Donald Trump has labeled a "hoax."
OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed cases in which their AI models slipped past safety controls, hid mistakes and hacked systems they were not meant to access.
How US, China could end the AI race
What did David Robinson write?
In an op-ed for The Atlantic, Robinson said AI needs guardrails similar to those for nuclear power and aviation, adding, "The time for trial and error is over."
He called for more emphasis on safety and research before US Big Tech develops more advanced AI models "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."
Robinson, who oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier AI-model launches, said the recent errors were typical because tech giants are prioritizing "speed and flexibility."
"An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."
The former OpenAI employee noted that the firm relies on "iterative deployment." It releases new AI models first and only tightens safeguards after problems show up.
"As ​the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the ​level of care ‌that I believe is needed," Robinson, who worked at OpenAI for 3 1/2 years, added.

blocks.caption: Activists have staged protests calling on AI labs to slow developmentImage: Karl Mondon/AFP

blocks.text: ChatGPT creator insists AI is safe

OpenAI reacted to the latest criticism in a statement, "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage ​and secure, and ⁠we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."
In recent months, there have been repeated warnings from technology experts and policymakers that AI models are advancing so fast they could take control and possibly wipe out humanity.
Despite those fears, US President Donald Trump is vehemently against stronger regulation, insisting that it will slow down innovation and make it harder for US AI models to beat Chinese rivals.
This week, Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet's Google.
The president described the deal as "morally binding,” even if it is not legally enforceable.
He also directed his administration to rename AI as "Super Intelligence" or SI.
A survey by Reuters/Ipsos last month found that three-quarters of Americans worry that AI giants are not doing enough to stop AI from causing serious harm to society.

articles.title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
articles.summary: For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.

image.caption: Taliban security forces after a Pakistani airstrike in Khost, September 2026Image: AFP

blocks.text: On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.
These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.

The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.
Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.

blocks.caption: Pakistani security officials inspect a mosque destroyed in an attack in the border town of Kohat, September 2026Image: Hussain Ali/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship

The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.

Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.
Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.

"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan

The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.

"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."
This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.
Difficult borders

There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.

The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.
So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.
"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.

In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.

"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.
Pakistan exerts pressure

Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.

blocks.caption: A Taliban soldier with an anti-aircraft gun on the border with Pakistan in April 2026Image: AFP

blocks.text: Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.

So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.

An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.

The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.

"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."
Significant escalation
This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.

British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.
Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.

"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.
Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan

In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times, Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.
The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.
"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.
In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.
This story was originally published in German.

articles.title: Tennessee's prison chief resigns after botched execution of murderer Christa Pike
articles.summary: Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike.

image.caption: Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a fellow student in 1995 [FILE: December 2007]Image: J. Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/USA TODAY NETWORK/REUTERS

blocks.text: The head of the prison system in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong, the state governor said Saturday.
Witnesses said Pike was still breathing and moaning after two doses of the anesthetic pentobarbital failed to kill her during Wednesday's procedure.
The attempt was halted and she was transferred to hospital in critical condition.
It was the second time this year that an execution in the southern state had to be halted.
What do we know about the resignation?
Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that prison commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post sometime this month.
Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
In the same statement, Strada acknowledged that: "Stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."
He said the department had carried out its responsibilities in accordance with established protocol, but called the review "entirely appropriate and necessary."
The state has halted further executions until the review has been completed.
Strada took on the role in January 2023. Nearly two years later, he announced that Tennessee would, from then on, only use pentobarbital for lethal injections of death-row inmates.
What went wrong?
Tennessee authorities have yet to explain why Pike survived.
Her attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike's lawyers said Friday that she is unconsciousand on a ventilator in hospital.
While they welcomed Strada's departure, her legal team said, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”
"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," the four-lawyer team said.
"We hope the governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system," it added.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state since 1820.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996, aged 20, for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convinced was trying to steal her boyfriend.
Slemmer, who was 19, was tortured and killed in a remote area near the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.

articles.title: Latvia election: Pro-Ukraine PM Kulbergs set to retain power after historic victory for his United List party
articles.summary: Latvia's prime minister looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.

image.caption: Centrist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (right) is the favorite, but his coalition is expected to emerge weakenedImage: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election.
The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition.
What do the results show?
With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said.

Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears

An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.
Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.
Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones. Despite his party leading opinion polls, his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.
Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.
Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.
Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats
German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace
Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.
Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.
Once ballots are fully counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.
Estonia and Latvia: Life on NATO's eastern edge

articles.title: Ukraine to step up oil attacks as Russia hits Kyiv bridges
articles.summary: As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.
articles.byline: Nik Martin, Wesley Dockery, Dharvi Vaid Dhulia

image.caption: A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro RiverImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday vowed to continue hitting Russia's oil refineries in retaliation for what he called Moscow's new strategy of targeting major Ukrainian cities for intensive air strikes.
Ukraine has accused the Kremlin of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent days, to force residents to leave urban areas of the country before winter.
In strikes over the past two days, Russian forces have also hit two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in the capital, Kyiv.
What did Zelenskyy say?
In an interview with Reuters news agency, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence agencies had uncovered details of a "new doctrine" from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelenskyy warned.

The Ukrainian leader said that Kyiv would "respond in any way (we can) ... First of all, oil refiners: who give money to them [Russia] for this war. But we will not respond, of course, like them, on any ‌civilian objects."
Second Kyiv bridge struck
This week marks the first time Moscow has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday that the Northern Bridge over the river was struck by Russian forces from the air.
In a statement posted on Telegram, Klitschko said two people were injured and the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged.
"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.
Over the past two days, Kyiv's Southern Bridge has been hit several times by a volley of strikes by Russian drones.
The attacks caused traffic chaos, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

blocks.caption: Cars were stuck in traffic jams on Friday after Russian attacks on the Southern BridgeImage: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

blocks.text: A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.
Russia urges foreign diplomats, nationals to leave Kyiv
Russia's Foreign Ministry on Saturday, meanwhile, warned foreign diplomats and nationals in Kyiv to leave the city, adding that "individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger."

"The Armed Forces of the Russian Federation will continue to deliver massive retaliatory strikes," it said, while adding that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning."
In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.
Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.
Putin on a war footing: escalation on all fronts?
Moldova denounces latest Russian strike on Ukraine
Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the latest Russian attack on Kyiv and complained about a violation of her country's airspace.
"Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu said in a post on X. "5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil."
"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," Sandu said.
The Moldovan Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and urged Moscow to prevent such incidents.
Moldova is a strong supporter of Ukraine, and its airspace is frequently violated due to Russian attacks on its neighbor.
Russian forces are stationed in the Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria, raising fears that Moldova could be the next target of invasion after Ukraine.

articles.title: US Coast Guard searches for missing air ambulance off coast of Massachusetts
articles.summary:
The plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contact

The US Coast Guard is searching for an air ambulance jet with six people onboard that…

blocks.text: The US Coast Guard is searching for an air ambulance jet with six people onboard that lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during a flight from Bermuda to Boston early on Saturday morning.
In a statement to the Guardian, an FAA spokesperson said that the agency issued a search-and-rescue alert notice for a Gulfstream G-100 at about 1.20am local time on Saturday.

The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers onboard when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade international airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport, obtained by the Associated Press.

NBC News reported that the plane was carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda, citing a statement from Clarence Togeretz, the director of flight operations at Latitude Air Ambulance, the aircraft’s operator.

“We always get rather concerned when our crew doesn’t report to us in a timely manner,” he told NBC News. “But I will say that again, optimistically and positively, that doesn’t mean that the worst has happened.”

NBC also reported that the Massachusetts port authority, which operates Boston Logan international airport, said the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled. A port authority spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with those onboard and their loved ones as the search continues.”
The FAA is coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the US Coast Guard to locate the aircraft.
The search area as of Saturday morning was off the coast of the island of Nantucket, Massachusetts, the coast guard said in a statement posted to X.
Air and surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft, the statement added.
Citing a source with knowledge of the investigation, ABC News reported there were no Americans onboard the plane, though the identities of those onboard were not immediately released.
Officials believe the plane rapidly descended 7,500ft before hitting the water, according to the outlet’s source.

articles.title: 4 Canadians aboard missing Ontario-based air ambulance flying from Bermuda to Boston

blocks.text: Air ambulance went missing early Saturday
The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for an Ontario-based air ambulance jet that has gone missing with six people on board while flying from Bermuda to Boston on Saturday.
The Gulfstream G100 jet with tail number C-GRJP is registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, a Hamilton-based air ambulance provider, according to the tracking website Flightradar24.

The company lost contact with the jet around 1:30 a.m.today, said Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude. The U.S. Coast Guard's northeast division said the Federal Aviation Administration also reported losing contact with the jet in the early hours of Saturday.

There were two pilots and two medical staff — all of whom are Canadian — on board. A patient and their relative were also on board. They are not Canadian and were picked up in Bermuda, Togeretz told CBC.
Togeretz said they are staying optimistic that everyone will be safely found.
Air and surface teams are searching for the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., the U.S. Coast Guard's northeast division said in a social media post.

The jet's last trip was from Hamilton to the North Atlantic island of Bermuda on Friday evening, according to flight history on Flightradar24. Before Friday and Saturday's flights, the jet had flown within Canada over the past week.
CBC News has contacted federal and provincial authorities for more information about the aircraft.

articles.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
articles.summary: The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

image.caption: Police forces across the UK have stepped up patrols outside synagogues [FILE: October 2, 2025]Image: Andrew Matthews/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.
The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.
What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, in northern England.
He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.
The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.
Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.
He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.
The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.
One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.
The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.
Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

blocks.caption: Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025]Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.
Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.
The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.
Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.
UK releases air base plot suspects

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.
UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.
Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.
The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.
Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.
Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title: Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
articles.summary: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.

blocks.text: US authorities are searching for six people after a medical plane bound for Boston, Massachusetts went missing early Saturday morning.
The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC that it lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane and put out a search and rescue notice just after 1:00 local time (6:00 GMT).
An air and water search is underway off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, according to the US Coast Guard's Northeast District.

The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was slated to land at Boston's Logan International at 1:30 EDT (6:30 GMT).
According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).

articles.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
articles.summary: Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.

image.caption: The latest wave of protests emerged in response to the forced eviction of an elderly woman in MadridImage: Alejandro Martinez Velez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.
The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.

"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.
They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.

blocks.caption: Protesters demanded affordable housingImage: Javier Soriano/AFP

blocks.text: "What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.
Protests in dozens of cities
Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.
Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.
In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.
Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.

blocks.caption: Protesters filled the streets of the Spanish capitalImage: Juan Barbosa/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's next for the Spanish government?

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.
This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.
"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators held signs calling for 'a right to a roof' among other slogansImage: Javier Soriano/AFP

blocks.text: Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decion.
Sahcnez's office declined to comment on the reports.

articles.title: Why has Brazil accused the US of election interference?
articles.summary: The Latin American country will vote for its next president, as Lula da Silva and Bolsonaro clash over sovereignty, security and ties with Washington.

blocks.text: In Brazil’s upcoming presidential election, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is facing right-wing challenger and ally of Donald Trump, Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Washington has backed closer ties with Brazil’s right wing, while Lula da Silva has accused Bolsonaro’s camp of encouraging foreign interference.
The election has raised questions about US influence, trade tariffs, organised crime and Brazil’s sovereignty.
The BBC's Ione Wells explains.

articles.title: Will Spain's housing crisis lead to a snap election?
articles.summary: The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is in Madrid, where a series of marches have been scheduled, after Spain's Congress rejected measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.

blocks.text: Thousands of people are continuing protests across Spain, after Congress rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.
Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by government in response to nationwide protests that followed the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home.

Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a rent increase by the company that owns her flat. The case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years.
The BBC's Guy Hedgecoe is at one of the protests in Madrid and looks at whether the government's defeat will lead to an early general election, which is not due until next summer.

articles.title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
articles.summary: More than 50 protests are planned to take place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.

blocks.text: The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenant's Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.
